# Chapter 1 - sketch answers {.unnumbered}

\(1\) Governance: The system by which the organisation is directed and
controlled - the FastGoods owner declaring customer-data protection a priority
and being answerable for it. Risk management: Identifying, assessing and
treating what could go wrong - FastGoods ranking R3 above a website typo and
choosing a treatment. Compliance: Meeting binding and adopted norms -
FastGoods honouring the GDPR because it holds personal data. (2) Governance: The
leadership's decisions on manual operation, communication and refusing the
ransom. Risk management: The backups, the insurance (a transfer of risk) and the
manual fallback (a reduction of impact), all arranged in advance. Compliance:
The stock-exchange notice and notification of authorities. None is a technical
control, because each is a decision or an obligation, not a mechanism. (3)
Asset: The customer database and the personal data in it. Threat: An attacker
seeking data to sell or misuse. Vulnerability: A weakness that exposes the
database - for instance an unpatched component or excessive access rights.
Risk: A breach - moderate likelihood, very high impact (customers harmed,
trust lost, GDPR duties triggered). Control: Reduce exposure, e.g. patching,
least-privilege access and encryption of the stored data. (4) GDPR: Binding -
a regulation that applies because personal data is held. ISO 27001
certification: Adopted - chosen, then committing. PCI DSS: Adopted through the
payment contract - but contractually enforceable, so binding in effect.
Password policy: Adopted - self-imposed, yet staff must follow it. Compliance
sets a floor defined for everyone in the same situation; being safe requires
controls matched to FastGoods' actual risks, and a box ticked on paper (an
unrestored backup, say) protects nothing. (5) Preventive: Traffic filtering or a
DDoS-protection service in front of the checkout. Detective: Monitoring and
alerting on abnormal traffic and checkout availability. Corrective: A recovery
procedure that restores the checkout, e.g. via the provider's mitigation and
standby capacity. All three defend availability.
